questions.question: Explain HTTP caching deeply — Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified — and how to implement it properly in Spring Boot.
questions.title: HTTP Caching: Cache-Control, ETags, Last-Modified
questions.direct_answer: HTTP caching has two main mechanisms: **freshness** (Cache-Control directives like `max-age`, `public`, `private`, `no-cache`, `no-store`, `immutable`) tell caches how long a response stays fresh without revalidation; **validation** (ETag, Last-Modified + If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since) lets a cache check with origin cheaply — 304 Not Modified if unchanged, saving bandwidth. Use together: set `Cache-Control: max-age=300, public` for fresh reuse; set ETag so stale caches revalidate cheaply. In Spring Boot: use `ResponseEntity.ok().cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(5, TimeUnit.MINUTES)).eTag(etag).body(...)` or `ShallowEtagHeaderFilter` for auto-ETags; combine with CDN (CloudFront, Cloudflare) and compression (Brotli > gzip) for real production wins.

interviewer_intent.testing: Deep understanding of HTTP semantics; practical caching strategy; real performance engineering
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting Cache-Control: no-cache everywhere (disables caching); returning wrong Vary headers (poisons CDN); generating weak ETags on dynamic data (no real savings)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss public vs private, stale-while-revalidate, stale-if-error, CDN integration, Vary header pitfalls, conditional requests, Brotli vs gzip, and cache key design

sections.title: HTTP Caching: Freshness and Validation
sections.content:
HTTP caching reduces origin load, tail latency, and bandwidth by reusing responses. The HTTP/1.1 RFC (RFC 9111) defines two mechanisms:

**Freshness** — 'how long can I reuse this response without asking the server?'
Set by `Cache-Control: max-age=300` (seconds) or `Expires: Tue, 22 Apr 2026 14:00:00 GMT` (older). While fresh, the cache serves without contacting origin.

**Validation** — 'this response is stale; is it still good?'
Set by `ETag: "abc123"` (opaque content hash) or `Last-Modified: Tue, 22 Apr 2026 10:00:00 GMT`.
- Cache sends conditional request with `If-None-Match: "abc123"` or `If-Modified-Since: ...`.
- Origin returns:
- **304 Not Modified** if unchanged — no body, cache's copy is still good; cheap for origin
- **200 OK + new body** if changed

Combined, these give the right behavior:
- `Cache-Control: max-age=60, public` + `ETag: "v1"` = 1-minute fresh window; after that, revalidate cheaply

**Directives that matter in 2026:**

- `public` — may be stored by shared caches (CDN, proxy)
- `private` — browser/user cache only; never CDN
- `max-age=N` — fresh for N seconds
- `s-maxage=N` — fresh for N seconds in shared caches (overrides max-age for CDN)
- `no-cache` — may cache but must revalidate before serving
- `no-store` — don't cache at all (secrets, PII)
- `must-revalidate` — don't serve stale even if origin is unreachable
- `immutable` — content will never change (versioned assets: `main.abc123.js`)
- `stale-while-revalidate=N` — serve stale for N seconds while revalidating in background
- `stale-if-error=N` — serve stale for N seconds if origin returns 5xx

**Three layers of cache** (all see the same headers):
1. **Browser cache** — per user
2. **CDN** (CloudFront, Cloudflare, Fastly) — edge pop, shared
3. **Origin / reverse proxy** (nginx, varnish) — in front of your servers

Good caching design is the cheapest performance win you'll ever get. A well-cached API can serve 99% of traffic from the edge without touching your Spring Boot servers.

sections.title: Spring Boot Implementation Patterns
Cache-Control Directive Deep Dive + Gotchas
sections.content:
**`no-cache` is not 'no caching'.** `no-cache` means 'store but must revalidate before serving'. `no-store` means 'don't store at all'. Huge difference. Use `no-store` for PII, auth tokens, credit card responses.

**`public` vs `private`.** `public` = any cache may store (CDN, proxy, browser). `private` = only browser/user cache. Never put `public` on user-specific data; CDN will serve to other users.

**`max-age=0, must-revalidate`.** Equivalent to `no-cache`. Response stored; revalidated on every request. Useful for frequently-changing content with cheap revalidation.

**Vary header pitfalls.** `Vary: *` effectively disables caching. `Vary: User-Agent` splits cache by browser (hundreds of variants; terrible hit rate). Be precise: `Vary: Accept-Encoding` is cheap; `Vary: Authorization` is needed for per-user; `Vary: Accept-Language` for localized.

**ETag strength.**
- **Strong ETag** (`"abc123"`): byte-for-byte identical
- **Weak ETag** (`W/"abc123"`): semantically equivalent

For APIs, weak ETags are fine. For range requests, strong required.

**ETag generation strategies.**
- Version field + updated_at hash (best, O(1))
- Content hash (MD5/SHA of serialized body; ShallowEtagHeaderFilter; O(body size))
- Incrementing revision number

Avoid regenerating on every request if expensive — defeats caching purpose.

**If-None-Match vs If-Match.** `If-None-Match` = 'send body only if ETag differs' (caching). `If-Match` = 'only process this request if ETag matches' (optimistic concurrency). Different headers, different semantics.

**Revalidation cost.** A 304 still costs a round trip. If origin is 100ms away and max-age=0, every request pays 100ms. Tune `max-age` to balance freshness vs round-trip cost.

**Stale-while-revalidate is a game changer.** Response fresh 30s; during next 5 min, serve stale immediately to user while revalidating in background. p99 latency drops dramatically; user never waits for revalidation. Supported by modern browsers and CDNs.

**Stale-if-error.** If origin returns 5xx during revalidation, serve stale for N more seconds. Buys you headroom during incidents. Combined with SWR, survives minor origin blips transparently.

**CDN cache keys.** Default: URL + Vary-specified headers. Query string may or may not be in key (configurable in CloudFront, Cloudflare). Auth header usually not in key; use `Vary: Authorization` if you cache per-user.

**CDN cache invalidation.** Purge by URL pattern. Expensive and slow on some CDNs. Prefer versioned URLs (asset.abc123.js) — change version, URL changes, old cached forever without harm.

**Compression: gzip vs Brotli.**
- **gzip**: universal; 70% reduction on JSON
- **Brotli**: 20–30% better compression; supported by all modern browsers; enable in CDN or nginx
- Both: Accept-Encoding negotiated; cache by Vary: Accept-Encoding

**Don't compress small responses.** Overhead > savings for < 1KB. Spring Boot's default `min-response-size: 1024` is sensible.

**Don't compress already-compressed (images, video).** No gain; wasted CPU.

**HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.** Multiplexing means many requests over one connection. Slightly different caching semantics (no Head-of-Line blocking). Same HTTP headers.

**Cache poisoning.** Attacker sends request that causes cache to store malicious response for others. Mitigations: validate Host header; use Vary correctly; don't cache based on user-controlled headers you don't expect.

**POST isn't cacheable by default.** Changing to GET or using idempotent POST with caching hints is rare. GraphQL's POST + query body is why its caching is hard.

**Cache-Control response vs request.** Request: `Cache-Control: no-cache` from client = force revalidation. Response: server instructs caches. Servers control, clients hint.

**Observability.** Dashboard:
- CDN hit rate (target > 80% for public content)
- Origin request rate (inverse of CDN effectiveness)
- 304 rate (indicates validation working)
- Average response size with and without compression

**Production pattern.**
- Static assets: `max-age=31536000, immutable` (1 year) + versioned URLs
- Rarely-changing API (product catalog): `max-age=300, public` + ETag + SWR
- User-specific data: `max-age=60, private` + Vary: Authorization
- Auth tokens, PII: `no-store`
- Tune per endpoint; measure hit rates; adjust

**Spring Boot's `ShallowEtagHeaderFilter` vs manual ETag.** Filter is easy but computes hash from full response body on each request; no origin work saved. Manual ETag (version/updated_at) avoids serialization entirely on 304. For expensive endpoints, manual.

**The strategic answer:**
- Cache-Control for freshness policy, ETag/Last-Modified for validation
- Use CDN with well-tuned headers — cheapest scaling win
- stale-while-revalidate + stale-if-error for resilience
- Versioned URLs for immutable assets; revalidation for dynamic
- Measure hit rates; tune; repeat

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Two mechanisms**: freshness (Cache-Control max-age) + validation (ETag / Last-Modified)
- **`no-cache` means 'revalidate'**, `no-store` means 'don't cache at all'
- **`public` vs `private`**: never put `public` on user-specific data (CDN will serve to others)
- **Vary header is critical**: `Vary: Accept-Encoding` cheap; `Vary: *` disables caching
- **ETag generation**: version + updated_at is O(1); content hash is O(body size)
- **`stale-while-revalidate`** is a huge p99 win — serve stale immediately, revalidate in background
- **`stale-if-error`** serves stale during origin 5xx; improves resilience
- **Immutable + versioned URLs** for assets: `main.abc123.js` with `max-age=1y, immutable`
- **Compression**: gzip ubiquitous, Brotli 20–30% better on modern browsers; don't compress < 1KB
- **Measure CDN hit rate** — target > 80% for public content; tune headers based on evidence

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HTTP caching reduces origin load, tail latency, and bandwidth by reusing responses. The HTTP/1.1 RFC defines two complementary mechanisms.

**Freshness — how long can I reuse without asking the server?**
- Set by Cache-Control max-age in seconds
- While fresh, cache serves without contacting origin
- Expires header is the older alternative

**Validation — this is stale, is it still good?**
- Set by ETag (opaque content hash) or Last-Modified timestamp
- Cache sends conditional request with If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since
- Origin returns 304 Not Modified if unchanged (no body, cheap) or 200 with new body if changed

**Combined they give the right behavior**
- max-age=60 plus ETag: fresh for 1 minute, then cheap revalidation
- Matches real-world data patterns

**Cache-Control directives that matter**
- public: any cache may store (CDN, proxy, browser)
- private: only browser; never CDN
- max-age=N: fresh for N seconds
- s-maxage=N: overrides max-age in shared caches (CDN)
- no-cache: may cache but must revalidate before serving
- no-store: don't cache at all (secrets, PII)
- must-revalidate: don't serve stale even if origin unreachable
- immutable: content never changes (versioned assets)
- stale-while-revalidate=N: serve stale for N seconds while revalidating in background
- stale-if-error=N: serve stale for N seconds if origin 5xx

**The three layers of cache**
- Browser cache: per user
- CDN: CloudFront, Cloudflare, Fastly; shared at edge
- Origin reverse proxy: nginx, Varnish
- All see the same headers; good design uses all three

**Common mistakes**

*no-cache is not 'no caching'*
- no-cache means 'store but revalidate before serving'
- no-store means 'don't cache at all'
- Huge difference; use no-store for PII and secrets

*public on user-specific data*
- CDN will serve one user's data to another
- Always private + Vary: Authorization for user-specific

*Vary header pitfalls*
- Vary: * effectively disables caching
- Vary: User-Agent splits cache into hundreds of variants
- Be precise: Accept-Encoding cheap; Authorization needed for per-user

*ETag generation cost*
- Content hash on every request means no CPU savings
- Better: version plus updated_at (O(1) generation)
- ShallowEtagHeaderFilter is easy but computes hash from full body

**Stale-while-revalidate is a game changer**
- Fresh 30 seconds; during next 5 minutes serve stale immediately, revalidate in background
- User never waits for revalidation
- p99 latency drops dramatically
- Supported by modern browsers and CDNs

**Stale-if-error for resilience**
- If origin returns 5xx during revalidation, serve stale for additional N seconds
- Buys headroom during incidents
- Combined with SWR, survives minor blips transparently

**Spring Boot patterns**

*Static assets with versioned URLs*
- main.abc123.js with max-age=1 year, immutable, public
- Change content means change URL; no invalidation needed

*API responses with ETag*
- ResponseEntity.ok().cacheControl(...).eTag(etag).body(p)
- WebRequest.checkNotModified(etag) compares If-None-Match and returns 304

*User-specific data*
- CacheControl.maxAge(60, SECONDS).cachePrivate()
- Vary: Authorization
- Browser caches per user; CDN doesn't cache

*Stale-while-revalidate*
- CacheControl.maxAge(30s).staleWhileRevalidate(5min).staleIfError(30min)
- Huge p99 wins for low-volume dynamic data

**Compression**
- gzip universal; 70% reduction on JSON
- Brotli 20 to 30% better than gzip; all modern browsers support
- Don't compress under 1KB; overhead exceeds savings
- Don't compress images or video; already compressed
- Vary: Accept-Encoding to cache per compression type

**CDN integration**
- Default cache key is URL plus Vary headers
- Invalidation by URL pattern; slow and expensive
- Prefer versioned URLs over manual invalidation
- Target CDN hit rate above 80% for public content

**Cache key design**
- Vary: Accept-Encoding is cheap and valuable
- Vary: Authorization for per-user cached content
- Avoid Vary: User-Agent unless you handle dozens of variants
- Query string handling configurable in CloudFront/Cloudflare

**The production pattern**
- Static assets: max-age=1 year, immutable, versioned URLs
- Rarely-changing API: max-age=5 min, public, ETag, stale-while-revalidate
- User-specific data: max-age=1 min, private, Vary: Authorization
- Auth tokens and PII: no-store
- Tune per endpoint; measure hit rates; adjust

**Observability**
- CDN hit rate (target > 80% for public content)
- Origin request rate (inverse of effectiveness)
- 304 response rate (shows validation working)
- Response size with and without compression

**The strategic answer**
- Cache-Control for freshness; ETag or Last-Modified for validation
- CDN with well-tuned headers is the cheapest scaling win
- stale-while-revalidate plus stale-if-error for resilience
- Versioned URLs for immutable assets
- Measure hit rates; tune; repeat
- Well-cached API serves 99% of traffic from edge without touching your Spring Boot servers

questions.question: How does HTTP response compression work (gzip, Brotli, zstd), and how do you configure it in Spring Boot without hurting latency?
questions.title: HTTP Compression — gzip, Brotli, zstd in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: HTTP compression is content-coding negotiated via **`Accept-Encoding`** (client) and **`Content-Encoding`** (server). The server picks one codec — **gzip** (universal), **Brotli** (30–50% smaller on text, browser-only), or **zstd** (fast and small, Chromium-only) — compresses the body, and sets `Content-Encoding`. In Spring Boot enable it with `server.compression.enabled=true`, whitelist text MIME types via `server.compression.mime-types`, and set `server.compression.min-response-size` around 1–2 KB so small payloads don't pay CPU cost for no byte savings. Already-compressed assets (JPEG/PNG/MP4/Parquet) must be excluded — re-compressing them costs CPU and grows bytes.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand HTTP content-coding negotiation (Accept-Encoding/Content-Encoding), know the three mainstream codecs (gzip/br/zstd) and their trade-offs, and can configure Spring Boot compression with a sensible min-size threshold and MIME-type allow-list.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Enabling compression globally with `min-response-size=0`, compressing tiny JSON responses and paying CPU for kilobytes saved; or compressing already-compressed content types (images, video) and inflating size. Also: serving compressed responses without a `Vary: Accept-Encoding` header, poisoning shared caches.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Brotli static vs dynamic modes, zstd support (Chromium 123+), precompressed static asset serving via `gzip_static`/`brotli_static`, HTTP/2 HPACK + body compression composition, and why TLS 1.3 closed the BREACH attack only for specific cases — secrets in reflected bodies still need mitigation.

sections.title: How HTTP Content-Coding Negotiation Works
sections.content:
Compression in HTTP is a **content-coding** — an end-to-end transformation of the response body.
- The client advertises what it can decode in **`Accept-Encoding`** (e.g. `gzip, br, zstd`), and the server picks one, compresses the body, and replies with **`Content-Encoding: br`**.
- If the server can't or won't compress, it omits `Content-Encoding` and returns the body verbatim.

Two practical rules govern this:
- The server **MUST** emit `Vary: Accept-Encoding` on any compressed response so intermediate caches (CDN, reverse proxy, browser cache) key the entry per encoding and don't serve a gzipped body to a client that asked for identity
- Compression happens **inside** TLS — the encrypted bytes on the wire are the compressed payload, so compressing the response saves both bandwidth and transfer time

Three codecs dominate in 2026:
- **gzip** — universal, ~30 years old, RFC 1952, ~3–5× compression on text, cheap CPU
- **Brotli (br)** — Google, RFC 7932, 15–30% better than gzip on text at similar CPU, supported by every modern browser and most CDNs; has a precomputed dictionary that makes small text payloads especially compact
- **zstd** — Facebook, RFC 8878, fastest at high compression ratios; Chromium 123+ sends `zstd` in `Accept-Encoding`, Firefox support is behind a flag as of mid-2026, safe to enable with content-negotiation fallback

sections.title: Spring Boot Configuration — application.yml
sections.content:
server:
  compression:
    enabled: true
    # Only compress content types that benefit — text and structured data
    mime-types:
      - application/json
      - application/xml
      - application/javascript
      - application/graphql+json
      - application/problem+json      # RFC 7807
      - text/html
      - text/xml
      - text/css
      - text/plain
      - image/svg+xml                   # text-like, compresses well
    # Below this size the CPU cost outweighs the byte savings
    min-response-size: 2KB
    # Exclude MIME types even if client asks — already-compressed
    excluded-user-agents: ''          # don't use unless you really must

# Reverse proxy / gateway note:
# If Nginx/Envoy/CloudFront already compresses upstream responses,
# disable Tomcat compression to avoid double work and double CPU.

sections.title: Per-Endpoint Override and curl Verification
sections.content:
# 1. Ask for gzip explicitly
curl -s -I -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' https://api.example.com/v1/orders
# HTTP/2 200
# content-type: application/json
# content-encoding: gzip
# vary: Accept-Encoding
# content-length: 1847   # compressed size

# 2. Ask for brotli — modern CDNs will respect it
curl -s -I -H 'Accept-Encoding: br' https://api.example.com/v1/orders
# content-encoding: br
# vary: Accept-Encoding

# 3. Ask for multiple with q-values; server picks best
curl -s -I -H 'Accept-Encoding: zstd;q=1.0, br;q=0.9, gzip;q=0.8' \
     https://api.example.com/v1/orders

# 4. Negotiation off -> identity response
curl -s -I -H 'Accept-Encoding: identity' https://api.example.com/v1/orders
# (no content-encoding header; raw body)

# 5. Decompress manually for debugging
curl -s -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' https://api.example.com/v1/orders | gunzip

# 6. Measure compression ratio on a real payload
for enc in identity gzip br; do
  bytes=$(curl -s -H "Accept-Encoding: $enc" -o /dev/null -w '%{size_download}' \
          https://api.example.com/v1/orders)
  echo "$enc: $bytes bytes"
done

sections.title: Programmatic Control — Disable Compression for One Endpoint
When Compression Helps — and When It Hurts
sections.content:
**Where compression is a clear win**
- JSON/XML API responses over 2 KB — typical ratios 3–8× for gzip, 4–10× for Brotli
- HTML, CSS, JavaScript bundles — Brotli static precompression on CDN edge gives best-in-class sizes
- GraphQL responses — usually large and highly repetitive (shared field names) so compress very well
- Server-side rendered pages and sitemaps

**Where compression hurts or is pointless**
- Already-compressed media — JPEG, PNG, WebP, MP4, Parquet, ZIP, JAR; recompressing wastes CPU and often grows bytes
- Tiny payloads (< 1–2 KB) — gzip header overhead (~18 bytes) plus the CPU cycle is worse than the savings
- Real-time streaming where TTFB matters more than bytes — gzip's deflate state must flush for each chunk, adding latency
- `Content-Encoding` on responses that should remain verbatim (e.g. pre-signed content served byte-identical)

**CPU budget**
- gzip level 6 (default) costs ~30–50 μs per KB on modern server CPUs
- Brotli dynamic at level 4 (good default for live responses) costs ~80–150 μs per KB; level 11 is for static precompression only
- zstd level 3 is close to gzip level 1 in CPU but compresses like gzip level 9

**Static vs dynamic compression**
- Static assets — precompress at build time (`gzip -9` + `brotli -q 11`), serve `.gz` / `.br` variants via `gzip_static on; brotli_static on;` in Nginx or `aws-cloudfront-compression=gzip,brotli`
- Dynamic JSON — compress on the fly at moderate level (gzip 6 / brotli 4); don't waste level 11 CPU on every request

**HTTP/2 + compression**
- HTTP/2's HPACK compresses headers; body compression is independent and composes normally
- HTTP/3 uses QPACK for headers; still unrelated to content coding

sections.title: Security, Caching, and Operational Gotchas
sections.content:
**`Vary: Accept-Encoding` is mandatory**
- Without it, a shared cache (CDN, browser) can serve a gzipped response to a client that sent `Accept-Encoding: identity`
- Spring Boot's Tomcat compression adds the `Vary` header automatically; verify with `curl -I` on every environment

**BREACH-style attacks**
- If secrets (CSRF tokens, session IDs) are reflected inside a compressed response body alongside attacker-controlled data, compressed-length side-channel attacks can leak them
- Mitigations: move secrets out of response bodies, add per-response random padding, disable compression on endpoints that reflect secrets, or rely on TLS 1.3 with per-request key derivation as partial defence
- TLS 1.3 did not eliminate BREACH — it only closed CRIME (TLS-level compression); body compression is still an attack surface

**Double compression**
- If the CDN (CloudFront, Fastly, Cloudflare) compresses edge responses, disable `server.compression.enabled` in Spring Boot — compressing twice is pure CPU waste
- Some proxies strip `Accept-Encoding` from upstream requests and recompress at the edge; check with `curl -I` through the full chain

**Streaming endpoints**
- Server-Sent Events and NDJSON generally should not be compressed — gzip has to flush its deflate state on every chunk boundary, destroying the latency benefit
- If you must, use `Content-Encoding: gzip` with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` and flush explicitly

**Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding**
- Dynamic compression usually switches the response to `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` because the final size is not known at header-write time
- Some clients or proxies mishandle chunked — verify, especially in corporate networks

**Reverse-proxy coordination**
- If Nginx/Envoy sits in front of Spring Boot and is configured with `gzip on` / `brotli on`, let the proxy compress — it's faster, usually precompiled against SIMD-accelerated libraries
- The Spring Boot service should then serve uncompressed, keeping CPU free for application logic

sections.title: Trade-offs — Codec and Level Selection
sections.content:
**Size vs CPU**
- Brotli dynamic level 4 — 10–20% smaller than gzip level 6, ~2–3× the CPU; reasonable for high-traffic APIs when bandwidth cost dominates
- gzip level 6 — the safe universal default; every client understands it
- gzip level 1 — trades ratio for speed; useful when CPU is constrained and payloads are large
- Brotli level 11 — 30–50% smaller than gzip; only viable for **static precompression** at build time

**Ratio vs latency**
- Compressing a 10 KB JSON at gzip 6 adds ~0.5 ms CPU and saves ~7 KB bandwidth — win at almost any network speed
- Compressing a 500 B JSON adds ~40 μs CPU and saves ~50 B — pure waste; hence `min-response-size: 2KB`

**Client coverage — 2026**
- `gzip` — 100% client coverage; always safe
- `br` — all modern browsers, most mobile HTTP libraries, curl 7.57+, Java 21 HttpClient with a module
- `zstd` — Chromium 123+ sends it by default; Firefox behind flag; enable only with `br`/`gzip` fallback via content negotiation

**When to disable entirely**
- Endpoints already serving pre-compressed assets (images, video, archives, Parquet)
- Latency-sensitive streaming (SSE, WebSocket upgrade responses, NDJSON bulk exports without buffering)
- Responses with secrets reflected inside attacker-controllable content (BREACH mitigation)
- Behind a CDN that already handles compression at the edge

**Observability**
- Log `Content-Length` and `Content-Encoding` — track average compression ratio by endpoint
- Alert when a normally-compressed endpoint starts returning `identity` — indicates configuration drift or a proxy stripping the header
- Track CPU time spent in the compression codec via JFR; over 5% of request CPU means your level is too high

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Content-coding negotiation** — `Accept-Encoding` (client), `Content-Encoding` (server), `Vary: Accept-Encoding` (mandatory on compressed responses for correct cache keying)
- **Three mainstream codecs in 2026** — gzip (universal), Brotli (better ratio, browser-centric), zstd (fastest, Chromium-first)
- **`server.compression.enabled=true` + MIME allow-list + `min-response-size: 2KB`** — the Spring Boot one-liner
- **Never compress already-compressed content** — JPEG/PNG/MP4/Parquet/ZIP; re-compression loses CPU and often grows bytes
- **Brotli level 11 is for static precompression only** — dynamic responses should use level 4 or gzip level 6
- **CDN vs origin** — if the edge compresses, disable origin compression to avoid double work
- **Streaming endpoints usually skip compression** — gzip's deflate-state flushing per chunk destroys the latency benefit
- **BREACH is still live** — don't reflect secrets inside compressed bodies with attacker-controlled input; TLS 1.3 did not eliminate this attack

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
HTTP compression is content-coding negotiated between client and server.

**How negotiation works**
- Client sends `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, zstd` — the list of codecs it can decode
- Server picks one, compresses the body, and replies with `Content-Encoding: br`
- Server must add `Vary: Accept-Encoding` so shared caches key per encoding; otherwise a CDN can serve a gzipped body to a client that only accepts identity

**Three codecs that matter in 2026**
- gzip — universal, cheap CPU, 3–5× on text; always safe
- Brotli — 15–30% better than gzip on text at comparable CPU; every modern browser supports it
- zstd — fastest, Chromium 123+ sends it; enable with brotli and gzip fallback

**Spring Boot configuration**
- `server.compression.enabled=true`
- `server.compression.mime-types` — allow-list text and structured data (JSON, XML, HTML, CSS, JS, SVG, application/problem+json)
- `server.compression.min-response-size: 2KB` — below that the CPU cost outweighs the savings
- Brotli is not built in — add `brotli4j` as a servlet filter if you need it at origin

**When compression hurts**
- Already-compressed media: JPEG, PNG, WebP, MP4, Parquet — skip them, or you grow bytes
- Tiny payloads under 1 KB — gzip header alone is ~18 bytes
- Streaming endpoints (SSE, NDJSON) — flushing deflate state per chunk kills latency
- Secrets reflected in bodies with attacker-controlled input — BREACH attack surface

**Static vs dynamic**
- Static assets — precompress at build time with Brotli level 11 and gzip -9; serve `.br` / `.gz` variants from the CDN
- Dynamic JSON — gzip level 6 or Brotli level 4; never level 11 on every request

**CDN coordination**
- If CloudFront, Fastly, or Cloudflare compresses at the edge, disable origin compression — don't double the work
- Verify with `curl -I` through the full chain that `Content-Encoding` and `Vary` are correct

**Verification**
- `curl -H 'Accept-Encoding: br' -I` — check `Content-Encoding` and `Vary`
- Measure ratios per endpoint in monitoring; alert when a normally-compressed endpoint starts returning identity — usually a proxy stripping the header

beats.text: Compression in HTTP is a content-coding — an end-to-end transformation of the response body. The client advertises what it can decode in Accept-Encoding (e.g. gzip, br, zstd), and the server picks one, compresses the body, and replies with Content-Encoding: br. If the server can't or won't compress, it omits Content-Encoding and returns the body verbatim. Two practical rules govern this: The server MUST emit Vary: Accept-Encoding on any compressed response so intermediate caches (CDN, reverse proxy, browser cache) key the entry per encoding and don't serve a gzipped body to.

steps: Where compression is a clear win JSON/XML API responses over 2 KB — typical ratios 3–8× for gzip, 4–10× for Brotli HTML, CSS, JavaScript bundles — Brotli static precompression on CDN edge gives best-in-class sizes GraphQL responses — usually large and highly repetitive (shared field names) so compress very well Server-side rendered pages and sitemaps Where compression hurts or is pointless Already-compressed media — JPEG, PNG, WebP, MP4, Parquet, ZIP, JAR; recompressing wastes CPU and often grows bytes Tiny payloads (< 1–2 KB) — gzip header overhead (~18 bytes) plus the CPU cycle is worse than the savings Real-time streaming where TTFB matters more than bytes — gzip's deflate state must flush for each chunk, adding latency Content-Encoding on responses that should remain verbatim (e.g.
pre-signed content served byte-identical) CPU budget gzip level 6 (default) costs ~30–50 μs per KB.
